============================================================================\n418: \n419: val_t rayTriangleIntersect(const Vec3& orig, const Vec3& dir,\n420:                             const Vec3& v0, const Vec3& v1, const Vec3& v2) {\n421:     Vec3 e1 = v1 - v0;\n422:     Vec3 e2 = v2 - v0;\n423:     Vec3 pvec = dir.cross(e2);\n424:     val_t det = e1.dot(pvec);\n425: \n426:     if if (u < 0.0f || u > 1.0f) return std::numeric_limits<val_t>::max();\n432: \n433:     Vec3 qvec = tvec.cross(e1);\n434:     val_t v = dir.dot(qvec) * invDet;\n435:     if (v < 0.0f || u + v > 1.0f) A pair consumes\n// SAMPLES_PER_PAIR draws unless it is culled (or i == j), so the stream position of\n// each pair depends on earlier pairs only through the cull decision. To keep the\n// results identical to a serial run while still using all cores, the stream is\n// generated in pair order by thread 0 one batch ahead, while all threads evaluate\n// the current batch in parallel. Each pair's Kij depends only on its own samples,\n// so the parallel evaluation order does not affect the output.\nvoid computeFormFactors(SimulationState& state) {\n    printf(\"Computing form factors (Kij)...\\n\");\n\n    const size_t N = state.numTriangles;\n    const size_t totalPairs = N * N;\n    const size_t batchSize = std::min(totalPairs, FORM_FACTOR_BATCH_PAIRS);\n    const size_t numBatches = (totalPairs + batchSize - 1) / batchSize;\n\n    RandomGenerator rng(42);\n\n    // Double-buffered sample storage and per-pair \"needs evaluation\" flags\n    std::vector<val_t> samples[2];\n    std::vector<uint8_t> active[2];\n    for (int b = 0; b < 2; ++b) {\n        samples[b].resize(batchSize * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR);\n        active[b].resize(batchSize);\n    }\n\n    // Generate samples for batch `batch` in serial stream order (called by one thread)\n    auto produce = [&](size_t batch) {\n        std::vector<val_t>& buf = samples[batch & 1];\n        std::vector<uint8_t>& act = active[batch & 1];\n        const size_t start = batch * batchSize;\n        const size_t count = std::min(batchSize, totalPairs - start);\n        for (size_t q = 0; q < count; ++q) {\n            const size_t f = start + q;\n            const size_t i = f / N;\n            const size_t j = f % N;\n            bool use = false;\n            // Cull triangles facing the same direction\n            if (i != j && state.triangles[i].normal().dot(state.triangles[j].normal()) <= 0.99f) {\n                use = true;\n            }\n            act[q] = use ? 1 : 0;\n            if (!use) continue;\n            val_t* dst = buf.data() + q * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR;\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < SAMPLES_PER_PAIR; ++k) {\n                dst[k] = rng.rand();\n            }\n        }\n    };\n\n    produce(0);\n\n    size_t rowsReported = 0;\n\n    #pragma omp parallel\n    {\n        const int tid = omp_get_thread_num();\n\n        for (size_t b = 0; b < numBatches; ++b) {\n            // Thread 0 prepares the next batch while the others evaluate this one\n            if (tid == 0 && b + 1 < numBatches) {\n                produce(b + 1);\n            }\n\n            const size_t start = b * batchSize;\n            const size_t count = std::min(batchSize, totalPairs - start);\n            const val_t* buf = samples[b & 1].data();\n            const uint8_t* act = active[b & 1].data();\n\n            #pragma omp for schedule(dynamic, 16)\n            for (long long q = 0; q < static_cast<long long>(count); ++q) {\n                if (!act[q]) continue;\n                const size_t f = start + static_cast<size_t>(q);\n                const size_t i = f / N;\n                const size_t j = f % N;\n                state.kij[f] = computeKijFromSamples(\n                    state.triangles[i], state.triangles[j],\n                    buf + static_cast<size_t>(q) * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR,\n                    state.octree, i, j);\n            }\n            // (implicit barrier above)\n\n            #pragma omp single\n            {\n                // Rows [0, rowsComplete) have all their pairs finished\n                const size_t rowsComplete = (start + count) / N;\n                for (; rowsReported < rowsComplete; ) {\n                    ++rowsReported;\n                    if (rowsReported % 100 == 0 || rowsReported == N) {\n                        printf(\"  Progress: %zu/%zu triangles\\n\", rowsReported, N);\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\nvoid computeTimeDelays(SimulationState& state) {\n    printf(\"Computing time delays (Tau)...\\n\");\n\n    const long long N = static_cast<long long>(state.numTriangles);\n    #pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)\n    for (long long i = 0; i < N; ++i) {\n        for (size_t j = 0; j < static_cast<size_t>(N); ++j) {\n            if (static_cast<size_t>(i) == j) continue;\n            state.tau[state.idx2d(static_cast<size_t>(i), j)] = computeTau(\n                state.triangles[static_cast<size_t>(i)], state.triangles[j]);\n        }\n    }\n}"},"output":"Edit applied successfully.","metadata":{"diagnostics":{},"diff":"Index: /home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/roomsim_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_omp_r5/roomsim/roomsim.cpp\n===================================================================\n--- /home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/roomsim_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_omp_r5/roomsim/roomsim.cpp\n+++ /home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/roomsim_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_omp_r5/roomsim/roomsim.cpp\n@@ -582,32 +582,118 @@\n // ============================================================================\n // Precomputation Phase\n // ============================================================================\n \n+// Number of (i,j) pairs per pipeline batch in the form factor computation\n+constexpr size_t FORM_FACTOR_BATCH_PAIRS = 16384;\n+constexpr size_t SAMPLES_PER_PAIR = 4 * NUM_RAYS;\n+\n+// The random samples come from one sequential mt19937 stream. With N=1280 rows split across 256 threads, each thread only handles 5 rows per timestep, so the per-barrier overhead probably dominates the actual work.\n\nMy rough math for the producer-consumer workload suggests the precomputation at 256 threads should take maybe 160ms, but it's actually taking 2 seconds, which points to either barrier wakeup latency (passive wait policy causing ~50µs+ delays) or the producer itself being slower than expected. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793104756366,"sessionID":"ses_e82a757e4ffe8DN6FB7Sm0hJjr","part":{"id":"prt_17d5f14e50017GfAzR8vwTOa1l","messageID":"msg_17d5f0f78001xarej23bAFG7ah","sessionID":"ses_e82a757e4ffe8DN6FB7Sm0hJjr","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm estimating timing: roughly 3.2ns per draw times 64 draws gives about 206ns per pair, scaling up to roughly 340ms serial producer time across 1280 batches, versus 1023ms with 64 threads—so I'm checking whether the consumer side at 64 threads (26000/64 ≈ 406) becomes the bottleneck instead.\n\nWith overlap, I'd expect the max of producer and consumer time, around 406ms, not the observed 1023ms. So I'm digging into other factors—batch barrier overhead, dynamic chunk scheduling, or thread-0 imbalance since it must produce the next batch (3.4ms) before joining the shared loop for the current batch, which pushes per-batch cost toward 4-5ms and still doesn't fully explain the gap to 1023ms.\n\nI'm checking whether chunk sizing or cache effects are inflating per-pair compute cost beyond the expected 16µs, or if there's false sharing on writes, but these seem negligible at dynamic chunk sizes of 16. Rather than keep speculating, I think it's better to instrument directly—vary batch size and chunk size at 64 threads and measure actual timing instead of reasoning from estimates.\n\nLooking at the numbers more carefully, 256 threads showing 389ms for simulation when expected inner-loop cost per timestep is only ~10µs per thread is pathological, pointing toward something like CFS scheduling latency or thread wake-up delay after barriers under oversubscription with the background job competing for a core.\n\nThe background job is likely corrupting my scaling measurements by preempting threads mid-barrier for several ms at a time, so I should kill it now to get clean numbers, and only rerun the large N=5120 reference run later once I'm done measuring scaling.\n\n","time":{"start":1793104745701,"end":1793104756316},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793105429204,"sessionID":"ses_e82a757e4ffe8DN6FB7Sm0hJjr","part":{"id":"prt_17d68dd8f001sKIkBHnprm2DAW","messageID":"msg_17d68d7d9001gs2oskeshfSzzs","sessionID":"ses_e82a757e4ffe8DN6FB7Sm0hJjr","type":"reasoning","text":"The producer is taking 10.4ms per batch instead of 3.4ms when consumers run concurrently, but hits 4ms when run alone, suggesting a 2.5x slowdown from contention. This smells like hyperthreading—if those 256 \"cores\" are really 128 physical cores with HT, the producer thread might be sharing a physical core with a consumer thread.\n\nSince the producer's cost at 10ms dominates the consumer's 4ms, the whole system is producer-bound. I'm considering fixes: speeding up the mt19937 generation itself (hard to vectorize the twist step), parallelizing via jump-ahead to let multiple threads generate different batches from known stream offsets, or splitting the producer into independent streams computed from cumulative draw counts per batch.\n\nBut scaling this up to larger N reveals the deeper issue — the consumer workload scales with N² while the producer scales linearly, so at N=5120 the producer's serial RNG bottleneck becomes the dominant cost even with hundreds of threads. That's the fundamental ceiling imposed by a single serial random stream.\n\nThe real question becomes whether exact bitwise equivalence is required for correctness, or whether a statistically-equivalent but different random sequence would satisfy \"equivalent semantics.\" Since any output comparison would fail if the random draws differ, I think preserving the exact sequence is the safer bet, which pushes toward needing real jump-ahead rather than just a faster producer. I'm also wondering if the 3.2ns per draw is inherent to mt19937's generate_canonical path or just an artifact of the benchmark's dependency chain.\n\nThinking about whether the twist step itself could be vectorized since elements within a block are mostly independent given the old state, but that's a substantial engineering effort for a modest speedup, and parallelizing across threads via precomputed per-batch states from checkpoints might be a more practical path forward.\n\nI'm also considering whether a GF(2) jump-ahead approach could work, which requires knowing the minimal polynomial of MT19937's state transition — but computing powers mod a degree-19937 polynomial is heavy. I recall MT19937's period comes from a primitive characteristic polynomial, though I'm not certain it's a simple trinomial, which makes this jump-ahead approach less straightforward than I'd hoped.\n\nThe minimal polynomial from the output bits should match the state transition's characteristic polynomial since the output map is observable, but I still need the exact raw state vectors (624 words at index 0, readable via std::mt19937's serialization) to combine properly, since the recurrence operates on whole 624-word blocks and a jump by k draws decomposes into block transitions plus a remainder.\n\nI'm now tracing through which bits actually get used in the twist operation — upper bit of mt[i] combined with lower 31 bits of mt[i+1] — and realizing the 19968-bit state really only carries 19937 bits of effective entropy, since the lower bits of mt[0] enter the recurrence in a way that's partially redundant. This transient subspace is a subtlety that complicates building a clean jump-ahead matrix.\n\nGiven the effort involved (polynomial exponentiation, state combination, verification — maybe 150 lines) versus the risk, I'm weighing whether it's worth it: current scaling tops out around 26-40x speedup depending on N, while jump-ahead parallelism could realistically push that to ~200x. I'm considering fallback options like a hand-rolled, vectorized MT19937 for modest gains, but splitting the producer across threads isn't viable since the stream is inherently sequential.\n\nWorking through the batch-boundary jump math concretely: with roughly 100 batches for N=1280, each jump covers about a million draws, and naive polynomial squaring for that exponent would cost around 5ms per squaring step, totaling far too much per batch. Precomputing powers of x up front helps, but even then each jump still costs roughly 50ms against only 4ms of actual consumer work per batch — so this jump-ahead approach ends up too slow to be worthwhile here.\n\nSwitching to a slab-based idea instead: assign each thread a contiguous range of pairs, do one jump per thread (not per batch), then let that thread generate sequentially within its own slab, avoiding any pipeline bottleneck. This requires a cheap preliminary parallel pass to count active pairs and compute each slab's starting offset so threads can jump directly to their assigned position.\n\nBut estimating the jump cost itself is concerning — precomputing the modular polynomial powers and doing the mulmods per thread adds roughly 0.3-0.5s of fixed overhead, which is fine for larger N but dominates for smaller N like 1280 where the ideal runtime is only ~0.1s. So this jump-based overhead becomes a real tradeoff against the pipeline approach depending on problem size.\n\nGiven the complexity and risk of the jump method versus its marginal benefit, I'm leaning toward sticking with the pipeline approach, trying to squeeze the producer's constant factor down if possible, and being upfront that the RNG stream is fundamentally sequential — parallelism helps well up to around 32 threads, but beyond that the serial generation becomes the bottleneck.\n\nBut a 1.0s floor at only 26x speedup on 256 cores would likely disappoint someone expecting maximum scalability, so I want to check whether contention is really the cause of the slowdown — maybe the producer thread is sharing a hyperthread core with a consumer, cutting its throughput. I consider whether separating raw integer generation from float conversion would help, but since the Mersenne Twister step itself dominates the cost, that's unlikely to move the needle much, and other workarounds like on-the-fly checkpointing or leapfrogging within blocks don't seem promising either.\n\nSo I'm now digging into the actual arithmetic: estimating that raw generation costs roughly 1ns and float conversion around 2ns, and wondering if a hand-rolled bit-level conversion could cut that in half by avoiding a true division in favor of a multiply, since the compiler won't optimize the division without fast-math flags. I trace through libstdc++'s actual generate_canonical algorithm for float with a 32-bit generator to see exactly how it computes the ratio and handles the edge case where the result rounds up to 1.0, so that any replacement I write reproduces its exact behavior bit-for-bit.\n\nThe conclusion is that the gain from this optimization is maybe 1.5x at best, not transformative, so I'm starting to weigh whether a more substantial change like implementing a jump-ahead scheme is worth the implementation effort.\n\nBerlekamp-Massey over GF(2) on the output bit sequence should recover the minimal polynomial efficiently using bitset XOR operations across the ~40000 needed terms, and checking that the degree matches 19937 confirms the chosen output bit carries the full linear recurrence. From there, the Haramoto et al. jump-ahead method computes x^k mod φ(x) to express the state after k steps as a linear combination of early states, giving an efficient way to skip ahead without stepping through every iteration.\n\nI'm not fully certain whether those old mt[0] bits truly vanish from the reachable state or just feed into mt[623] and persist, which makes the 19937-vs-19968 discrepancy tricky to resolve analytically. Given that uncertainty, the safest path is empirical: compare jumped states against sequential stepping across many seeds and k values to confirm the matrix relation actually holds on the reachable subspace.\n\nI'm going to time-box this investigation and abandon implementing jump-ahead for now, instead accepting the pipeline design and looking for cheap wins: using a division-free RNG-to-float conversion verified for exact equivalence, and investigating whether the producer thread is being slowed by hyperthread contention with consumer threads sharing the same physical core. I want to check lscpu to see threads-per-core and test whether isolating the producer on its own core gets it back to full speed.\n\n","time":{"start":1793105386895,"end":1793105429125},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

That floor suggests the producer is now the bottleneck at 64+ threads, so the real lever left is speeding up the producer itself.\n\nSince the barrier forces batch time to be max(producer, consumers), and consumers only need ~2ms per batch at 128 threads while the producer needs ~4ms, lookahead buffering wouldn't actually raise throughput -- it'd just smooth out sync stalls, since the producer's total work time of 0.4s is the hard bound either way.\n\nParallelizing the twist itself across threads doesn't help much since twist dominates generation cost over tempering/float conversion. The fundamental issue is that the sequential RNG stream creates an inherent producer bottleneck without jump-ahead, which becomes even more pronounced at scale—at N=5120 with 256 threads, the producer could be the limiting factor by a factor of roughly 3.5x. I think I'll just document this limitation rather than try to fully engineer around it.\n\nParallelizing the producer without jump-ahead seems genuinely impossible—the twist operation is inherently sequential, and any approach to precompute starting states for parallel producer threads just requires running serially first anyway. A pair consumes\n// SAMPLES_PER_PAIR draws unless it is culled (or i == j), so the stream position of\n// each pair depends on earlier pairs only through the cull decision. To keep the\n// results identical to a serial run while still using all cores, the stream is\n// generated in pair order by thread 0 one batch ahead, while all threads evaluate\n// the current batch in parallel. Each pair's Kij depends only on its own samples,\n// so the parallel evaluation order does not affect the output.\nvoid computeFormFactors(SimulationState& state) {\n    printf(\"Computing form factors (Kij)...\\n\");\n\n    const size_t N = state.numTriangles;\n    const size_t totalPairs = N * N;\n    const size_t batchSize = std::min(totalPairs, FORM_FACTOR_BATCH_PAIRS);\n    const size_t numBatches = (totalPairs + batchSize - 1) / batchSize;\n\n    RandomGenerator rng(42);\n\n    // Double-buffered sample storage and per-pair \"needs evaluation\" flags\n    std::vector<val_t> samples[2];\n    std::vector<uint8_t> active[2];\n    for (int b = 0; b < 2; ++b) {\n        samples[b].resize(batchSize * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR);\n        active[b].resize(batchSize);\n    }\n\n    // Generate samples for batch `batch` in serial stream order (called by one thread)\n    auto produce = [&](size_t batch) {\n        std::vector<val_t>& buf = samples[batch & 1];\n        std::vector<uint8_t>& act = active[batch & 1];\n        const size_t start = batch * batchSize;\n        const size_t count = std::min(batchSize, totalPairs - start);\n        for (size_t q = 0; q < count; ++q) {\n            const size_t f = start + q;\n            const size_t i = f / N;\n            const size_t j = f % N;\n            bool use = false;\n            // Cull triangles facing the same direction\n            if (i != j && !(state.triangles[i].normal().dot(state.triangles[j].normal()) > 0.99f)) {\n                use = true;\n            }\n            act[q] = use ? 1 : 0;\n            if (!use) continue;\n            val_t* dst = buf.data() + q * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR;\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < SAMPLES_PER_PAIR; ++k) {\n                dst[k] = rng.rand();\n            }\n        }\n    };\n\n    produce(0);\n\n    size_t rowsReported = 0;\n\n    #pragma omp parallel\n    {\n        const int tid = omp_get_thread_num();\n\n        for (size_t b = 0; b < numBatches; ++b) {\n            // Thread 0 prepares the next batch while the others evaluate this one\n            if (tid == 0 && b + 1 < numBatches) {\n                produce(b + 1);\n            }\n\n            const size_t start = b * batchSize;\n            const size_t count = std::min(batchSize, totalPairs - start);\n            const val_t* buf = samples[b & 1].data();\n            const uint8_t* act = active[b & 1].data();\n\n            #pragma omp for schedule(dynamic, 16)\n            for (long long q = 0; q < static_cast<long long>(count); ++q) {\n                if (!act[q]) continue;\n                const size_t f = start + static_cast<size_t>(q);\n                const size_t i = f / N;\n                const size_t j = f % N;\n                state.kij[f] = computeKijFromSamples(\n                    state.triangles[i], state.triangles[j],\n                    buf + static_cast<size_t>(q) * SAMPLES_PER_PAIR,\n                    state.octree, i, j);\n            }\n            // (implicit barrier above)\n\n            #pragma omp single\n            {\n                // Rows [0, rowsComplete) have all their pairs finished\n                const size_t rowsComplete = (start + count) / N;\n                for (;
